newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Mold looms over Vietnam robusta coffee crop.
newsitem.headline: Mold looms over Vietnam robusta coffee crop.

text.p: Moldy beans may become a problem for Vietnam's robusta coffee crop if rains pounding the country persist for a few more weeks, regional traders said on Wednesday.

"It's not a good situation in Dak Lak. You can deal with moisture problems, but when you start getting into moldy beans, you can't fix it. It could be quite a serious problem for the robusta market," a European trading house trader told Reuters.
"Moldy beans are a very strong possibility," another trader who recently visited Dak Lak said. "It can be a problem."
Dak Lak produces about two-thirds of the estimated 270,000 tonnes of robusta coffee beans exported annually by Vietnam.
Another dealer with a U.S. trading house was more cautious, saying it is still too early to say if coffee beans coming from Vietnam's highlands will be hit by mold.
"I think if the rains continue for two to three more weeks, it may become a problem," the trader said. "The weather is beginning to show better signs. Conditions should be better in December."

The rains have also made transportation of the beans to the southern port of Ho Chi Minh city difficult, traders said. The chances of mold increases because almost all of the beans are transported in jute sacks or plastic bags.
Shipments of coffee beans for the month of October were down sharply and were estimated to have reached about 10,000-15,000 tonnes against 15,000-17,000 tonnes in the same month last year.
In November, shipments will probably reach only 16,000-20,000 tonnes compared with 26,000-30,000 tonnes in the same month in 1995, dealers said.
Vietnam's benchmark Grade 2 robusta coffee beans were priced by regional traders at around $1,070-$1,090 a tonne FOB Saigon for prompt shipment, almost unchanged from last week.
The price of the same grade of coffee was steady at about $1,090-$1,100 a tonne FOB Saigon for December shipment.
